title: Can Agentic AI Develop Embedded Systems with Model-Based Design?
summary: MathWorks shows an agent building an inverted-pendulum controller inside a Simulink workflow, arguing that agents should follow established engineering processes, reuse verified tools and test early rather than one-shot vibe coding.

assertions.quote: this was a collaborative iterative process. We guided the agent step by step. We reviewed what it produced

verdicts.note: Small batches with fast feedback are a strong DORA predictor of delivery performance; DORA 2024 linked AI to larger batches and lower stability.

assertions.quote: if you don't think about exactly what you want in quantifiable and verifiable ways, then you don't know how to direct the agent

verdicts.note: Clear requirements, examples and references reliably improve agent output; the caveat is that bloated context can hurt, so curation matters.

Two practitioner grey sources say fuller context (requirements docs, examples, API docs, constraints) reduces ambiguity, and 40% of RQ2 sources report explicit context provisioning, but the review finds no comparison against ad-hoc prompting.
Airbnb: complex files only succeeded once prompts grew to 40-100K tokens with up to 50 related files, few-shot examples and migration guidelines, which proved 'highly effective'.

assertions.quote: Simulink generated embedded code from a model using well-tested, deterministic workflows. So, the same design always produces the same code.

verdicts.note: Migration case studies (Google, Amazon Java upgrades, Airbnb) got their scale from pairing LLMs with deterministic tooling and validation rather than free-form generation.

Google migration experience report: simple LLM prompting alone only works for the simplest migrations; AST tooling, heuristics and LLMs together are needed, and AST checks catch model mistakes cheaply and deterministically.

assertions.quote: we were able to test early and often. We can catch errors at a point in the process where it's still easy to fix them.

verdicts.note: Agent benchmarks and practice consistently show verifiable feedback (tests, compilers) is the main driver of agent success.

72% of 43 workflow sources put validation pipelines (tests, lint, runtime checks) at the core of the loop, and the review concludes quality 'seems to depend on the strength of the evaluation loop'; this is a frequency of mentions, and workflow comparisons are limited.

Google: every LLM edit goes through a build and unit-test loop with ML-powered repair of failures, and validation across several steps can 'recover' imperfect first attempts; this is the core of their migration pipeline.
Airbnb modelled its Enzyme->RTL migration as a state machine gated on Jest, ESLint and tsc, and retrying with the validation errors fed back fixed most simple-to-medium files within 10 attempts.

assertions.quote: why following proven engineering workflows matter even more when AI is involved

verdicts.note: DORA 2025 found AI amplifies existing engineering practices; strong fundamentals predict AI benefit.

assertions.quote: The problem, though, with this approach, at least for engineering problems, is that you're skipping the process that makes the result trustworthy.

verdicts.note: Unreviewed AI-built apps commonly ship with security, scaling and maintainability problems; prototypes are their sweet spot.

assertions.quote: this is something that Naren and I were able to verify was correct through our own expertise and understanding of the problem

verdicts.note: Studies show novices accept incorrect AI code more often; verifying output requires domain and code literacy.

Google RCT authors suggest heavier coders gain more from AI because current tools require spending much time verifying and editing generated code (interaction beta=-0.29, not significant), so coding skill conditions the benefit.

METR 2025: 75% of experienced developers read every line of AI code, 56% often make major cleanups, and 100% report needing to modify it; this shows correction is routinely needed, but the study does not test less-skilled users.

The Task 1 developer's Java proficiency influenced downstream outcomes more than AI use, and authors conclude human expertise still matters; qualitative quotes describe using experience to catch hacky AI suggestions.

Anthropic: the 'paradox of supervision' (supervising Claude needs the coding skills overuse may erode), and a security engineer saw a 'dangerously smart' proposal that only experienced judgment could catch.
